title: Switch, enum class, and the Ternary Operator
summary: Pick one of many branches with switch, switch over a scoped enum class, and choose between two values in one expression with ?:.
intro: An `else if` chain that tests one variable against many values gets long fast. A `switch` handles that case cleanly, an `enum class` gives the values names, and the ternary operator `?:` picks between two values in a single expression.

steps.title: switch, case, and break

example.title: Day of the week
example.prompt: Turn a day number from 1 to 7 into its name, with a default for anything else.
example.explanation: `day` is 3, so control jumps to `case 3:`, prints `Wednesday`, and `break` leaves the switch. The other cases never run. If `day` were 9, no label would match and `default` would print `Invalid day`.

practice.title: Game menu
practice.prompt:
Turn a menu option number into its label with a switch.

1. Keep the line that prints `Option 2: ` without a newline.
2. Switch on `option`: 1 prints `New game`, 2 prints `Load game`, 3 prints `Settings`, 4 prints `Quit`.
3. Add a `default` that prints `Unknown option`.
4. End every case with `break` and every label with `'\n'`.

Expected output:

```text
Option 2: Load game
```
hints: Copy the shape of the day example: one `case` per number, each ending with `break;`.
If you see `Load game` followed by `Settings`, a `break` is missing after case 2.

steps.title: Grouped cases and fallthrough

example.title: Grade feedback
example.prompt: Print feedback for a letter grade, where an A also counts as a pass.
example.explanation: `grade` is `'A'`, so the braced `case 'A'` body runs. Its `stars` variable lives only inside those braces. There is no `break`, so control falls into the shared `'B'` / `'C'` body, which prints `Passed`, then `break` exits. The `[[fallthrough]];` line only marks that as intentional. A `'C'` would print only `Passed`.

practice.title: Role permissions
practice.prompt:
Print every permission a user role has, where higher roles fall through to the lower ones.

1. Keep the line that prints `Role: e`.
2. Switch on `role` with stacked labels: `'a'` or `'A'` prints `Manage users`, `'e'` or `'E'` prints `Edit posts`, `'v'` or `'V'` prints `Read posts`.
3. Admin falls through to edit, and edit falls through to view, each marked with `[[fallthrough]];`. View ends with `break`.
4. Any other role prints `No access`.

Expected output:

```text
Role: e
Edit posts
Read posts
```

tests.output:
Role: e
Edit posts
Read posts

hints: Write `case 'e':` and `case 'E':` on two lines above the same body.
Only the view body needs `break`. The admin and edit bodies end with `[[fallthrough]];`.

steps.title: enum class and switch
steps.body:
An `enum class` defines a new type with a fixed set of named values. It turns magic numbers like `case 2:` into readable names. Define it above `main`.

```cpp
enum class Size { Small, Medium, Large };

const Size order = Size::Medium;
```

- The values are scoped: write `Size::Small`, never plain `Small`, so two enums can both have a `Small` without clashing.
- Under the hood each value is an `int` numbered from 0 (`Small` is 0, `Medium` 1, `Large` 2), so `sizeof(Size)` is 4. The names cost nothing at run time.
- The values do not convert to `int` on their own. `int n = Size::Large;` and `std::cout << Size::Large;` do not compile. Ask for the number with `static_cast<int>(Size::Large)`.

A switch over an enum class uses the scoped names as labels. If you list every value and leave out `default`, g++ with `-Wall` warns when you later add a value and forget its case.

example.title: Traffic light
example.prompt: Print which color a traffic light shows next, then print the number behind Green.
example.explanation: `current` is `Light::Yellow`, so the `case Light::Yellow:` body prints `Next: Red`. Every value has a case, so no `default` is needed. `Green` is the third value, so `static_cast<int>` turns it into 2.

practice.title: Compass turn
practice.prompt:
Print where you face after turning right, then print the number behind South.

1. Switch on `facing` with one `case` per `Direction` value.
2. A right turn goes North to East, East to South, South to West, and West to North. Print `Turn right: ` followed by the new direction.
3. After the switch, print `South is ` followed by `static_cast<int>(Direction::South)`.

Expected output:

```text
Turn right: North
South is 2
```
hints: Case labels use the scoped names, like `case Direction::West:`.
`std::cout << Direction::South` does not compile. Wrap it in `static_cast<int>(...)`.

steps.title: Choosing a value with ? :

example.title: Signs, prices, and plurals
example.prompt: Use ternaries to describe a number, find its absolute value, pick a ticket price, and choose singular or plural words.
example.explanation: `n >= 0` is false, so the first ternary yields `"negative"`. `absValue` is a `const` set in one line because the ternary hands back `-n`, which is 4. For `age` 70 the outer test `age < 12` fails, so the nested ternary runs and picks 7. The plural ternaries pick `"item"` only when the count is exactly 1.

practice.title: Shop status
practice.prompt:
Use ternaries to report a shop's stock, shipping cost, a number's sign, and file counts.

1. Print `in stock` when `stock > 0`, otherwise `sold out`, with a ternary inside `std::cout`.
2. Declare `const int shipping` as 0 when `total >= 50`, otherwise 5, and print `shipping: ` followed by it.
3. Declare `const char sign` as `'+'` when `x > 0`, `'-'` when `x < 0`, otherwise `'0'`, using one nested ternary, and print `sign: ` followed by it.
4. Print `1 file` and `4 files`, choosing the word with a ternary on each count.

Expected output:

```text
sold out
shipping: 5
sign: 0
1 file
4 files
```

tests.output:
sold out
shipping: 5
sign: 0
1 file
4 files

hints: Follow the example line by line: each task has a matching line there.
Put parentheses around every ternary you print, like `(n == 1 ? "file" : "files")`.
For the sign, put a second ternary in parentheses as the false branch of the first: `x > 0 ? '+' : (...)`.

recap:
- `switch (value)` jumps to the matching `case`. Labels must be constants, and the value must be an integer, `char`, or enum, never a `std::string` or `double`.
- End each case with `break`. A missing `break` falls through, so mark intentional fallthrough with `[[fallthrough]];`.
- Stack labels like `case 'y': case 'Y':` to share a body, and brace a case body that declares a variable.
- `enum class Name { A, B };` makes scoped values used as `Name::A`. They need `static_cast<int>` to become numbers.
- `cond ? a : b` is an expression: it can initialize a `const`, needs parentheses inside `std::cout`, and needs compatible types in both branches.
- Nest a ternary one level at most. Use `if` / `else` when the branches do work.
